Executive Summary

This is a 2006-built, 5-bed/4-bath home in Dublin's Sonata HOA community, originally inspected April 3, 2026. A follow-up reinspection was performed by the same inspector (CBI / Todd Erickson) on May 6, 2026 to verify completion of seller repairs. A subsequent set of seller repair photos (received May 9, 2026) documents substantially more work than the May 6 reinspection captured — including all four Section 1 termite items, plus several additional repairs not previously in scope. The current verified repair count stands at 13 inspection items repaired plus all 4 termite Section 1 items repaired, with photo evidence also showing four bonus repairs: the primary bathroom tub re-caulked, primary bedroom closet shelves installed, the conventional wall oven replaced (alongside the microwave), and the downstairs half-bath toilet replaced. 5 inspection items remain open: the cooktop center burner, two tub diverter valves, garage door safety sensors mounted too high, side gates dragging, and the upper-most bathroom under-sink shelf. 1 item was not addressed: the main electrical panel remains padlocked. Outside the inspection scope, the larger transactional concerns remain — the Sunrun solar PPA running to 2047 at $172/month, the HOA insurance policy renewal status, the 15-year-old roof with solar penetrations, and the 2010-vintage HVAC and AC approaching end-of-life. The HOA itself is financially healthy with reserves 97.5% funded. The seller's repair record at this stage is exceptionally strong — most of the financially significant items have been addressed before contingency removal.

Photo-Verification Walkthrough Checklist

At final walkthrough, work through this list and confirm each photographed repair in person. Bring this advisory and the original PDF on your phone for side-by-side comparison.

  • Page 1: Run water in primary bath left sink (drains normally?) + inspect tub caulk lines for clean tooling
  • Page 2: Open garage door from inside (does it self-close + self-latch?) + run water in primary bath right sink (no leak under cabinet?) + load-test closet shelves with hand pressure
  • Page 3: Heat water in microwave for 60 seconds + run a bake cycle on the new oven + obtain warranty paperwork for both
  • Page 4: Visually inspect chimney trimmer area from yard — confirm waterproofing + paint, not just bare wood; flush half-bath toilet, check base for leaks; confirm primary bath plumbing dry under sink; inspect kitchen sink cabinet rail repaint
  • Page 5: Open primary bath vanity cabinet — verify clean new substrate, no fungus residue, no water staining
  • Page 6: Open loft/upper bath vanity — verify same as above; visually inspect repaired window trimmers from outside (paint + flashing, not bare wood)
  • Page 7: Inspect window trimmers from yard at multiple windows; confirm garage side door area sealed with no water entry path
  • Pages 8–9: Look at front porch corner, garage interior, water heater closet, exterior siding above garage door for clean drywall/siding patches
  • Page 10: Visually inspect sliding door trim from outside; plug a phone charger into kitchen island and counter outlets to confirm power; turn on vent hood, listen for clean operation, look up to confirm new filters in place
  • Documentation to obtain at or before close: Section 1 Notice of Completion / clearance letter (covers all 4 termite items); manufacturer warranty registration paperwork for the new microwave and oven; main electrical panel key; any supplemental termite report relating to 3D chimney trimmer

High Priority — Safety & Significant Defects

Address before or at close of escrow — request seller repair or credit
I-01
No Carbon Monoxide Detectors Anywhere in the Home
Safety / Legal Repaired
California law requires CO alarms on each level of any home with a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage. This home has a gas furnace, gas cooktop, gas water heater, gas fireplace, and an attached garage — CO detectors are legally mandated and their absence is a required disclosure item at point of sale.
Verified May 6, 2026: Revised CBI report explicitly states "Carbon monoxide alarms are installed in the home on each level." Confirm at walkthrough that detectors are CA State Fire Marshal-listed.
I-02
Garage Fire-Wall Door Latch Broken — Door Will Not Self-Close or Latch
Fire Safety Repaired
The door between the living space and the garage (a fire-rated door required by code) has a stuck latch — it does not hold closed and cannot self-latch when shut. This door is required by building code to be self-closing and self-latching to contain a garage fire and prevent toxic fumes from entering the living space.
From original April 3 inspection — condition has since been corrected.
Verified May 6, 2026: Latch repair confirmed — item removed from the revised report. Test door at final walkthrough to confirm self-closing and self-latching action.
I-03
Main Electrical Panel Padlocked — Inspector Could Not Access or Evaluate
High Not Addressed
The 200-amp main electrical panel at the exterior left front corner was padlocked shut — no key was provided or found. The inspector was completely unable to evaluate the main panel's interior condition, breaker labeling, wire sizing, or any deficiencies. A home's main panel is one of the most critical systems to inspect.
  • Additionally, the home has a photovoltaic solar system connected to this panel — solar interconnection wiring, backfeed breakers, and any solar-related modifications inside the panel were also uninspectable
  • The subpanel in the garage was inspected and found serviceable with proper wire sizing and grounding
Demand the seller provide panel access (key) for a re-inspection before contingency removal. Hire an independent licensed electrician specifically to inspect the main panel interior — including solar backfeed connections, breaker condition, and overall panel integrity. Budget $150–$300 for this specialist inspection.
Status May 6, 2026: Panel remained padlocked at reinspection. The revised report repeats the same notation: "The main panel has a padlock on the cover and a key was not provided and one was not found in the home." This item has not been addressed — request seller provide the panel key before contingency removal.
I-04
3 Kitchen Outlets Dead — No Power (2 at Sink + 1 on Island)
High Repaired
Two outlets on the left side of the kitchen sink and one outlet on the kitchen island had no power. Other kitchen outlets and both GFCI outlets were functional.
From original April 3 inspection — condition has since been corrected.
Verified May 6, 2026: Item removed from revised report. Outlets restored. Confirm power at all three positions during walkthrough.
I-05
Open Junction Boxes in Two Bedroom Ceilings — Code Violation
High Repaired
Open (uncovered) junction boxes were found in the ceiling of the uppermost bedroom and the mid-level rear bedroom. All junction boxes must have covers per electrical code — exposed live wiring connections are a fire and shock hazard.
From original April 3 inspection — condition has since been corrected.
Verified May 6, 2026: Junction boxes covered. Item removed from revised report.
I-06
Moisture Damage to 3 Exterior Wood Trim Locations — Potential Mold Risk
High Repaired
Active moisture damage was found at three locations on exterior wood trim:
  • Garage side door jamb — moisture damage
  • Kitchen window trim board — moisture damage
  • Sliding door trim board — moisture damage
The inspector noted a separate pest/infestation report covers some of this damage as Section 1 fungus (see Termite tab item 3A and 3B). A ¾" unsealed hole in siding above the garage side door (old camera mount) was also noted.
From original April 3 inspection — condition has since been corrected.
Verified May 6, 2026: All three trim locations and the siding hole are removed from the revised inspection report. Damaged wood was replaced by general contractor and the camera-mount hole was sealed. Note: The Section 1 termite items 3A (window trimmers $1,495) and 3B (garage door casing $395) are separate findings from the termite report and remain to be remediated as part of the seller's termite obligation.
I-07
HVAC Furnace & AC Compressor Both Original 2010 — End-of-Life Approaching
High Cost Risk HVAC — Informational
Both major HVAC components are 15–16 years old:
  • Furnace: 2010 model, 88,000 BTU, attic-mounted. Typical life 20–25 years → 5–10 years remaining at best. Heat exchanger condition could not be evaluated by the inspector — requires a separate diagnostic by an HVAC contractor. A cracked heat exchanger produces lethal carbon monoxide.
  • AC Compressor: 2010 model, 4-ton split system. Typical life 18–23 years → could fail within 2–7 years.
Both units were operational at time of inspection, but age alone is a significant cost risk.
Hire an HVAC contractor (separate from the home inspector) to perform a diagnostic on both units, specifically including a heat exchanger crack test on the furnace. Use findings as basis for a price negotiation credit — combined replacement cost is $10,000–$18,000+. This is a legitimate item for seller credit.

Termite & Pest Inspection — Money Saver Termite

Inspected April 1, 2026 by Tom Maduell (OPR 6763) / Money Saver Termite, Pleasanton CA (925-922-4105). Report #20210546. This was a Complete Report — the highest scope level. The good news: no termites of any kind were found — no subterranean, no drywood. The finding was limited to Fungus/Dryrot only, with four items identified as Section 1 (active damage). In California real estate, Section 1 items are conventionally the seller's responsibility to remediate before close. Total quoted cost was $4,885.

📸 Status as of May 9, 2026: The seller has provided photo evidence documenting completion of all four Section 1 items — window trimmers (3A), garage door casing (3B), bath vanity shelves (3C), and chimney trimmer (3D). Recommend obtaining the formal Section 1 Notice of Completion / clearance letter from Money Saver Termite (or the contractor that performed the work) before contingency removal, and inspecting the work areas at final walkthrough.

⚠️ What "Section 1" Means: All four fungus findings are Section 1 — defined by California law as conditions where active infestation, infection, or damage is present on the date of inspection. This is the most serious classification. Section 1 items carry a strong conventional expectation that the seller pays for remediation in California transactions. Do not allow seller to credit instead of repair unless you've obtained independent bids confirming actual cost and scope.
🔗 Cross-Reference — Three Reports, Same Damage: These fungus findings directly confirm what both the CBI home inspection AND the HOA advisory flagged independently. The same locations appear across all three documents: garage door casing moisture damage, window trim moisture damage, and bathroom vanity shelf damage. This triple-confirmation means the damage is real, documented, and cannot be explained away. The termite report adds one entirely new finding — the Chimney Trimmer (3D) at $1,895 — which the home inspector missed entirely, likely because it required specialist access.

Cost Risk

In your seller repair request, include language requiring the seller to authorize and fund any supplemental scope discovered during execution of the Section 1 work — not just the quoted $4,885.

Overall Assessment — Post Reinspection & May 9 Photo Evidence

This is a substantive, well-located Dublin home in a financially healthy HOA. The structure is sound, the systems are functional, and the HOA is nearly 100% reserve-funded. The seller's cooperation on repairs has been exceptional — well above the typical seller response in California resale. The May 6 reinspection confirmed 13 of 15 actionable inspection items repaired. The May 9 seller photo set then documents all four Section 1 termite items remediated ($4,885 in work) plus four bonus repairs not in the original scope (primary bath tub re-caulked, primary closet shelves installed, conventional oven replaced, downstairs half-bath toilet replaced).

What still requires attention before close (six items, all minor): (1) the cooktop center burner — the only item the revised CBI report carries into its summary, (2) two tub diverter valves, (3) garage door safety sensors mounted too high, (4) two side gates dragging, (5) the upper-most bathroom under-sink shelf cosmetic damage, and (6) the main electrical panel padlock (panel key still not provided). Combined remaining repair scope is approximately $500–$1,200 in handyman work plus a brief electrician visit.

Documentation still to obtain: (a) Section 1 Notice of Completion / clearance letter from a licensed structural pest control operator covering all four termite items, (b) any supplemental termite report issued during the work (especially relevant to 3D chimney trimmer), (c) main panel key from seller, (d) Sunrun buyer approval and NEM2 transfer confirmation, (e) current HOA insurance certificate, (f) seller's roof and pest inspection reports if not already received.

Outside the repair scope but still on the buyer's plate: Sunrun PPA assumption to 2047 ($172/month), the 15-year-old roof with solar penetrations (independent roofing inspection still recommended), the 2010-vintage HVAC and AC approaching end-of-life (independent HVAC diagnostic still recommended for credit negotiation), and standard buyer move-in items.

Bottom line: The seller's repair record at this stage is unusually strong. The combined cost to finalize remaining items is modest, and the path to contingency removal is now mostly about documentation and walkthrough verification rather than negotiation over substantive defects.
